articles.title: Cameroon Food Security Outlook Update, October 2026 - May 2027: Conflict compounded by rainfall deficits to sustain elevated assistance needs through May
articles.description: Please refer to the attached file. Key Messages Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected to be widespread across the Northwest and Southwest regions from November 2026 through at least May 2027. Persistent insecurity, including kidnapping and protracted displacement, will continue to disrupt livelihoods and limit access to food and income. Reduced humanitarian assistance is expected to deepen food consumption gaps. A small but growing share of the worst-affected households are expected to face Emergency (IPC Phase 4) outcomes. In the Far North’s Mayo-Sava, Mayo-Tsanaga, and Logone-et-Chari, main harvests will improve food access, but conflict-related livelihood disruptions will keep outcomes Stressed (IPC Phase 2). Very poor refugee and displaced households with severely eroded livelihoods will remain in Crisis (IPC Phase 3). From February to at least May, early stock depletion, high food prices, and insecurity are expected to worsen outcomes to Crisis (IPC Phase 3), with some households facing Emergency (IPC Phase 4). FEWS NET projects that 1.5–1.99 million people will need humanitarian food assistance between October 2026 and May 2027, mainly refugees, internally displaced persons (IDPs), and conflict-affected households, with rainfall deficits exacerbating needs. Assistance needs are expected to increase countrywide and peak during the March–May 2027 lean season as market dependence grows amid weak purchasing power and high food prices. In the Far North, needs will likely ease through January 2027 after the main harvest before increasing again later in the outlook period. Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes are expected to persist through May 2027 in Mberé (Adamawa), Kadey (East), and Lom-et-Djérem (East), driven by pressure on local resources associated with the presence of refugees from the Central African Republic (CAR). Very poor refugee households are likely to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse outcomes. Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes are also expected to persist among poor urban displaced households in Yaoundé and Douala, where livelihood opportunities remain limited. In Mayo-Kani and Mayo-Danay, rainfall-related production shortfalls are expected to contribute to Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes among some households. The analysis in this report is based on information available as of October 23, 2026.

articles.title: DR Congo: Democratic Republic of Congo: IPC Acute Food Insecurity Snapshot | September 2026 – June 2027
articles.description: Please refer to the attached Infographic. Overview The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continues to face a severe food security crisis amid persistent conflict in the east, large-scale population displacement, and the expansion of Ebola, alongside climate and economic shocks. Worsening conditions in the east and northeast offset slight improvements in other areas of the country. Approximately 28.8 million people, representing 23 percent of the population analysed, are experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above) between September and December 2026. More than 3.6 million people (3 percent) are facing Emergency conditions (IPC Phase 4), marked by large food consumption gaps and elevated levels of acute malnutrition. While the national proportion of the population in Phase 3 or above is only marginally higher than in the previous analysis, conditions have deteriorated more markedly in the north-eastern and eastern provinces. North Kivu, South Kivu and Ituri remain the hardest-hit provinces, with 10.4 million people in Phase 3 or above; within these provinces, the territories of Djugu, Fizi, Shabunda and Walungu are classified in Phase 4. Internally displaced persons (IDPs), returnees, refugees, and poor households remain the most affected. In eastern DRC, conflict and violence continue to drive displacement, disrupt livelihoods and restrict access to food and markets. A rapidly expanding Ebola outbreak, recurrent disease epidemics, rising food and fuel prices, and the impacts of floods and other climate shocks are compounding vulnerabilities, leaving millions of people with limited means to meet their basic food needs. The food security situation is expected to worsen slightly from January to June 2027, with 30.3 million people (23 percent) projected to face Phase 3 or above, including 4.2 million people likely to face Phase 4. This represents an increase of nearly 1.5 million people in Phase 3 or above compared with the current period, driven by continued conflict and displacement, the spread of Ebola, and the anticipated impacts of El Niño, including flooding that could disrupt agricultural production and market access. Rising food, fuel and agricultural input prices are expected to place further pressure on vulnerable households, while declining humanitarian assistance and limited coping capacity increase the risk of further deterioration in food security conditions.
